utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-98-33-A, the Prosecutor versus Radislav Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Appearances. For the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour, my name is Christopher Staker, I appear for the Prosecution with my colleague Mr. Xavier Tracol, and our case manager is Ms. Nicola Bonfield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. And for General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a Status Conference called in accordance with Rule 65 bis. Is there anything which the Prosecution wishes to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. A status report was filed earlier this week, which sets out the current position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. I'm very grateful for that. It is a helpful document. Anything that the Defence wishes to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Norman Sepenuk, Your Honour. Just very briefly on General Krstic's medical condition. I'm sure Your Honour is aware that he had his leg amputated below the knee. He's had several surgeries, the last of which was in February 2001. Since that time he's had great difficulties with his leg, considerable pain, an infection in the area of the amputation. General Krstic would like, if possible, to have the surgeon who performed the February 2001 surgery come and see him. He has never -- the surgeon has never visited him since the surgery. I did call the detention centre this morning. Mr. McFadden wasn't there. I spoke to his assistant and he told me that General Krstic should speak to Dr. Falke, I believe it is, who might arrange for the visit of the surgeon. I left my name and number with the detention centre to pass along to Dr. Falke. This is not by way of any kind of complaint, Your Honour. I think General Krstic is generally pleased with the treatment he's received at the detention centre but his medical condition, particularly more recently, has deteriorated and he is undergoing a considerable amount of pain, and hopefully something can be done about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, this was raised at the previous Status Conference. Mr. Petrusic said it was matter they were going to raise with the Registry. Now, you may or may not be aware, but there's a particular procedure laid down in relation to the Detention Unit that you have to deal first of all with the superintendent or whatever title Mr. McFadden has, and then if you aren't satisfied with that, then you make a complaint to the president. But one thing the Chamber has no control over are matters within the Detention Unit. I don't know whether the doctor you refer to is the Dutch doctor who, like so many Dutch doctors, believes the body will heal itself, but it would be unfortunate if your client is having an infection and nothing is being done about it. But I really can't say any more than that you will just have to take the matter up with the superintendent, and if he is not able to assist you, then you have to make a complaint to the president. I hope, though, that if only for the selfish reason that we don't want the general to be in the hospital at the time we're hearing the appeal, that something is done about it pretty soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And we'll follow through with the detention centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I should add I had not asked General Krstic whether he could hear the proceedings in a language which he understood, because every time I asked him that, he stands up and I don't want him to have to go through that rather painful process, but I'm sure he can hear it, so that's all right. There's a question that arises about the Rule 115 material. There are a number of questions which arise about it. Since you filed your previous application and the addendum, there's been further material disclosed to you by the Prosecution, so the status report discloses to us. Do you propose to file a further application under Rule 115?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: We're not sure, Your Honour. We're trying to interview one further witness that hasn't been mentioned in our previous submissions who may be added to our Rule 115 list, but we're trying to interview that person very shortly, and the Prosecution has been very helpful in arranging that, and as soon as -- and that should take place, I would say, certainly within the next week. Mr. Petrusic? Yes. Sometime within the next week or so. Hopefully within the next week. Two weeks at the most. And then we'll know at that time whether we'll be adding him to our list or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: In your previous material, you said there were four witnesses. This is a fifth one, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: This would be a fifth one, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And have you got any further problems about the four that -- you were having some problems about finding them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: There are two witnesses. One is what we call Mr. Mercenary. That's the supplemental motion which we filed. I believe it was on January 10th, and it was a statement we had -- actually a little bit later than that, but we received the statement on January the 10th. This is a gentleman, again we don't know his name yet, but we call him Mr. Mercenary, and again the Prosecution has been very helpful in helping us to arrange an interview. The other person, Mr. Mimunovic, we have real problems there. We have now sent Mr. Amir Ahmic, the Bosnian liaison officer for the Prosecution, two letters requesting Mr. Mimunovic to talk to us, and we've given him written questions. He does not want to talk to us, and so we will eventually, probably quite soon, try to -- try to get the help of the Court in doing that. There's also a gentleman named Galic who also refuses to talk to Mr. Petrusic, and we may need the assistance of the Court in arranging for him to talk to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you understand, as the Prosecution has pointed out in relation to some of the existing witnesses, that it's no good just standing there -- standing back and saying, "They won't talk to us." You do have to demonstrate that you have attempted to follow all of the procedures there are available to you. Whether those procedures will assist in the end doesn't matter, you've got to try. For example, subpoenas and things like that. There is a very real problem, as you yourself have pointed out in your replies, that many of the processes which are available to the -- to an accused require you to demonstrate that the witness will be able to give evidence which assists your case. That's a fair point, but I'm not sure that every one of the procedures that are available would do so. I don't want you to sit back on that point and just do nothing. If you come along and you seek to have a subpoena issued because you have credible material which demonstrates this witness will assist you, not just on a fishing expedition but that you've got something that you really think that he can say, I would have thought that would have been sufficient under Rule 54 to get some sort of an order that he attend. Now, he may not comply with it, of course, but you really do have to do more than just say, "Well, they won't talk to us."

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we have laid the foundation out, particularly with Mr. Mimunovic, by sending two letters, not getting any answers, and our view is now to proceed with subpoena. The difficulty, though, and it may be just my own ignorance of procedures, although I must say I've asked around quite a bit amongst my brethren in the Defence bar at least, and they -- you can't subpoena someone, as I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. understand it, to your office, for example. You must subpoena that person to the court. And if the person continues to refuse to speak to us, if he simply shows up in court cold, it would be very difficult indeed, and I would say unwise in the extreme for Mr. Petrusic and I to start questioning in front of Your Honour and the other Appeals Court Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Nobody would expect you to do that. Taking depositions, I think you call it in the United States, a procedure whereby you can go along and ask anybody anything in someone's office certainly is not available here. Nevertheless, if you get him here, the witness will - assume that they turn up - will be asked by the Judge why he won't assist. You can get some assistance, even if it's of a psychological nature, as to why the witness won't cooperate. And it may go so far as establishing beyond any doubt that he won't cooperate. That's the sort of thing that you've just got to try. Try everything. It's no good standing back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the deposition point, if I may, you're saying that it's clearly not available? Because that was one of -- the Prosecution, in its response brief, said that that was also an available procedure under Rule 71.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Rule 71, depositions, where the evidence is taken, not that they come along and just be asked any question in some sort of private sphere that nobody else gets to know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. I would be willing -- on the deposition point, we're perfectly happy to have the government present when we interview this person. We simply want to know what he has to say. We don't particularly care about doing this ex parte. We would be happy, if it would help, to have the government present at an interview or at a deposition. We have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Your word deposition, like so many words in the English language, differs from what we understand it to mean. Your deposition is something which you just go along to find out what the witness is going to say. Our deposition is where the evidence which is actually tendered in the trial is taken, and it's usually because the witness can't come here because of illness or some disability. And that's a very different thing. The Rule 71 to which the Prosecution refers is certainly not what you're after. And indeed, the Prosecution is going to have a hard time persuading me, at least, that Rule 71 has got anything to do with it, unless the witness merely says, "I do not want to come to The Hague because I fear flying or I fear being arrested and safe conduct won't suffice so far as I'm concerned." Then there may be a case for taking his evidence - and that means the evidence that's going to be tendered at the trial - back in Yugoslavia somewhere, if I may so refer to the country as such. So you shouldn't get confused over this word "deposition."

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will -- our intention now is to follow up on what Your Honour has said and try to get the assistance of the Court with a subpoena. Again, the necessity thing is what has been the hurdle for us, showing necessity when the person won't even talk to us, but we will proceed in that way, and perhaps when a subpoena is served he might change his mind and agree to talk to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He may. But you see, Rule 54 is not limited in the way in which I think you are reading it. 54 says: "Necessary for the purposes of an investigation or for the preparation or conduct of the trial." Well, preparation would be, I would think, include finding out what this witness can say. But it would not be appropriate for us to have to sit down and listen while you probe him. We either use some form of moral coercion upon him to talk to you or we have to have it done in some other way. I think we all need to look at this from rather a fresh viewpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I very much appreciate Your Honour's comments, and we will follow up on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, I think I drew attention to this on the last occasion: Although, according to the Rules, the old Rule 115 applies to these proceedings, which allowed applications to be made up to 15 days before the hearing of the appeal, I want to make it very clear that's not going to apply in this case. We will not fix a date for hearing until the Rule 115 material has been sorted out. And at some stage, perhaps after the first stage of the proceedings when we say what we think is capable of altering the Trial Chamber's decision, we're going to have to find out from you how long you need to do the final preparation for the hearing so we can say, all right, we'll have a hearing in two weeks or three weeks' time, this sort of thing. Now, the Rule 115 material is under way. I must say it hasn't been made any easier both by the failure by the Defence to really give us very much assistance as to their due diligence, and also by the Prosecution's usual blanket response in almost the same terms in every case without applying very much consideration to the particular witness or documents that we have to consider, but it is under way and hopefully it will be given -- a decision -- the primary decision will be given reasonably shortly. But quite apart from Rule 115, there is the other issue I raised on the previous occasion and that was your complaint that you were prejudiced by the failure of the Prosecution to comply with Rule 68 during the trial. Now, obviously some of the material that has been produced now is material which you've tendered under Rule 115. So we understand that. We don't have to consider it otherwise but under Rule 115. But there may be cases, and we don't know from anything you've put before us so far, where you are going to complain about the failure to comply with Rule 68 because if, it had been complied with, you would have had avenues of investigation disclosed to you or something. Now, we really need to have some better particulars from you as to what you're going to do in relation to Rule 68. Mr. Farrell raised it on the last occasion and I did say to you we wanted to know something about it. We haven't got anything yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the Appeals Chamber's permission, perhaps the way to do it, if you'll let us, is to submit an additional -- to put an additional submission on that issue, because what we did is we combined Rule 68 with Rule 115, and there was one portion of our Rule 115 motion in which we set out all of what we regard as Rule 68 violations, and these were all the pre-judgement interviews. However, in thinking about it, perhaps that's an unfair burden to ask the Court to assume, and I would be very happy -- we would be very happy to file a brief spelling that out. We've just set forth the various Rule 68 violations. We would be happy to spell it out in more detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I hope your gestures aren't suggesting that you're going to file a brief about a foot thick.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's only the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But the -- it would be of assistance, because if we are able to read that sort of material in advance, it will save a great deal of time at the hearing where we may have to pursue the issue with you in more detail. So we would be grateful. I hope it's only an elaboration on what is the particular prejudice in relation to each of the documents which you haven't tendered under Rule 115 but which you say nevertheless there was a breach which caused you prejudice. The mere breach under Rule 68 won't get you a new trial or anything like that unless there has been a prejudice to your client's case. Well, I think those are all the matters I want to raise with you, unless there's something else you want to add, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No, it's just that we're grateful for the opportunity to make that submission, and I take it Your Honour will at some point, either now or in some written order, tell us how much time we have to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: How long do you need to put that document in? I'm hoping it's not going to be very large.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No, it's going to be short. My problem is I'm cramped on time a bit in the States and -- can we submit it by the 10th of April?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. You don't need a formal order for that, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No. And Mr. Staker, I think when the time arises, we will probably consult your alter ego to see how long he needs to decide how long he needs to reply to it. Mr. Farrell has got now a double-barreled action on this. He wants time to consider before he tells us how long he needs. So we'll worry about that, without any formal orders, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. One modest amendment. Could we make it the 11th of April?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, 11th of April. But Mr. Staker, there is another problem about 115. We're going to keep on having problems with Rule 115. There is a passage in the Kupreskic judgement to which Mr. Farrell is firmly wedded. It's in paragraph 63, and it talks about applying a relatively low threshold for credibility in admitting additional evidence with the issue of its weight being decided at a later stage. Now, the Rule has been amended, not, if I may say so, terribly well, since the Kupreskic decision, and it now says in Rule 115(B): "If the Appeals Chamber finds that the additional evidence was not available at the trial and is relevant and credible, it will determine if it could have been a decisive factor." Now, that's obviously the first stage of the procedure. And that word "credible" seems to be something a little bit -- requires something a little bit more than a relatively low threshold of credibility. And it's interesting to see that in the Kupreskic decision, in paragraph 63, it is introduced by these words: "The most appropriate course it was felt at the time was to apply a relatively low threshold for credibility." Now, in Kupreskic, despite the fact that there were 20-something applications for the admission of additional evidence, they ended up with three pieces, I think it was, and it was a very simple matter for the Appeals Chamber to determine all of that during the course of the hearing of the appeal. But since then, Rule 115 has taken off with a life of its own which nobody could ever have foreseen. And in the Blaskic case, for example, there is a very real possibility there may have to be a new trial ordered because there is no way in which an Appeals Chamber can conduct what might be regarded as a limited form of rehearing upon a small number of pieces of evidence. And it seems to me that this relatively low threshold for credibility is going to have to be looked at again in the context of the way in which the Rule is now written. And it may be that we're going to have to devise some system whereby we don't just exclude from the material tendered by the appellant all of that which was available at the trial, hasn't been -- hasn't led to a miscarriage of justice, and all of those -- what might be regarded as easy tests in most circumstances, and then have about 50 witnesses that are going to be cross-examined by the Prosecution in order to determine whether it could have been a decisive factor. And I'm hoping that the Prosecution will give some thought, as indeed the Defence, to what is the best possible way of dealing with it. It may be that we could exclude everybody or include -- perhaps that's a better way of putting it: Include everybody about which there is some, on the face of it, prospect of passing the test subject to cross-examination, so we can reduce the number of witnesses who are going to be cross-examined. It's a very large task for the Prosecution to have to be ready to cross-examine everybody who has been put forward in these documents. So would you pass it on to Mr. Farrell, who I know is absent because he's on duty elsewhere, that perhaps in his spare time that he has so much of he would like to give some consideration to this, because at some stage I'm going to ask both parties to make some submissions about it. I don't want you to have to answer now. It's not your case. But I think it's a matter we're going to have to consider to make this more manageable. Indeed, I propose to recommend that we have some reconsideration of the wording of the Rule. It's not going to save us in this case, but it really is not working well. So will you pass that on?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, is there anything else you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. Well, I'm very grateful to the parties. I think that perhaps it might be best from the Defence point of view if they do speak to Mr. McFadden rather than just the local Dutch doctor and say that somebody who is suffering from infection so long after an operation is clearly entitled to proper medical assistance. Whether that entails pulling the surgeon out to come out to the Detention Unit or not, I don't know, but it doesn't seem that he's getting proper medical attention if he is still having an infection so long after. And you might like to pass on to Mr. McFadden, who I believe is very helpful on these sorts of things, that we will expect him to come up with some sort of a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm grateful to the parties for their attendance, and I'll now adjourn.
